title: 𝛾-Bridge: A Look-Parametric Diffusion Bridge

paper.title: γ \gamma -Bridge: A Look-Parametric Diffusion Bridge
paper.abstract: Abstract Multiplicative Gamma noise is a signal-dependent degradation in coherent imaging; synthetic aperture radar (SAR) despeckling is its most prominent real-world instance. Existing diffusion denoisers parameterize their forward process by abstract signal-to-noise schedules rather than by the physical look number L L , so different deployment scenarios typically require separately trained models, and transfer from synthetic Gamma training to real SAR remains challenging without clean ground truth. We introduce γ \gamma -Bridge, a look-parametric bridge whose schedule L ⁡ ( t ) L(t) connects the noisy observation at L obs L_{\mathrm{obs}} to the clean limit through exact multiplicative Gamma marginals. Its closed-form Gamma–Lévy reverse posterior admits both stochastic and deterministic processes, while observation conditioning and a two-step consistency loss stabilize multi-step inference in the low-SNR single-look regime. Because bridge time directly represents L L , one conditioned network can smart-start from any admissible input look and stop at a target look number. These two orthogonal controls enable zero-shot restoration over the full admissible grid after training only at L obs = 1 L_{\mathrm{obs}}=1 on natural images with synthetic Gamma corruption. Combined with a homogeneous-patch look estimator, γ \gamma -Bridge processes data from six spaceborne and airborne SAR sensors without sensor-specific fine-tuning, achieving leading results on standard synthetic benchmarks while providing physically interpretable input and output controls absent from prior denoisers. Codes are released here .

sections.heading: I Introduction
sections.text: Multiplicative Gamma noise is a signal-dependent degradation encountered in coherent imaging systems, where it can obscure fine structures and radiometric information. Unlike additive Gaussian noise, its multiplicative and signal-dependent nature makes restoration a distinct image-processing problem. Synthetic aperture radar (SAR) despeckling is a major real-world instance and our primary validation setting. A SAR intensity image is commonly modeled as Y = X ⋅ N Y=X\cdot N , where X X denotes the underlying radar reflectivity and N N is unit-mean Gamma noise with variance 1 / L 1/L . The equivalent number of looks L L determines the noise strength; L = 1 L=1 corresponds to intensity formed from single-look complex (SLC) data at approximately 0 0 dB per-pixel SNR, while multi-look averaging or repeat-pass compositing increases L L , producing cleaner observations at the cost of spatial or temporal resolution. Gamma image restoration has been studied using both model-based and learning-based approaches. Classical log-domain optimization and fractional-diffusion methods suppress Gamma noise while preserving image structures [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . Diffusion-based methods include SAR-DDPM [ 4 ] , SDDPM [ 5 ] , and S 4 DM [ 6 ] , which employ Gaussian or transformed-domain diffusion processes. DDGM [ 7 ] introduces additive Gamma noise, while [ 8 ] formulate Gamma denoising through Beta-thinning. Recent studies unwind speckle with pretrained Gaussian denoisers [ 9 ] , or offer adjustable diffusion-equation smoothing [ 10 ] . However, their diffusion coordinates or control variables are not explicitly exposed as an inference-time axis parameterized by the physical look number. Existing methods generally assume a fixed restoration endpoint or adjust generic smoothing strength, and therefore cannot independently specify the input and output Gamma noise levels through ( L in , L out ) (L_{\mathrm{in}},L_{\mathrm{out}}) at inference time. A further difficulty is that real SAR scenes lack paired speckled and speckle-free ground truth. Supervised learning with synthetic Gamma corruption provides exact targets [ 11 , 12 ] , but may suffer from a gap between idealized noise and sensor- or processing-dependent real SAR statistics [ 13 ] . Semi- and self-supervised methods reduce the need for clean references, yet representative approaches rely on multi-temporal observations, complex-valued measurements, or blind-spot independence assumptions [ 14 , 15 ] . Per-image zero-shot methods avoid external training data but require image-specific optimization and still return a fixed restoration endpoint [ 16 , 17 ] . Thus, label-free inference alone does not establish zero-shot transfer from controlled Gamma training to heterogeneous real SAR sensors without fine-tuning. Since clean real-SAR references remain unavailable, such transfer must also be assessed through distributional and no-reference evidence. This work introduces γ \gamma -Bridge, a look-parametric bridge for general Gamma image restoration, with SAR as its primary real-world application and validation setting. Building on the Gamma-marginal construction of [ 8 ] and image-to-image diffusion bridges [ 18 ] , this work defines a look-number schedule satisfying L ⁡ ( 0 ) = L max L(0)=L_{\mathrm{max}} and L ⁡ ( T − 1 ) = L obs L(T{-}1)=L_{\mathrm{obs}} . Each intermediate state follows x t | x 0 ∼ x 0 ⋅ Gamma ⁡ ( L ⁡ ( t ) , L ⁡ ( t ) ) x_{t}\mid x_{0}\sim x_{0}\cdot\mathrm{Gamma}(L(t),L(t)) and therefore remains consistent with the standard L ⁡ ( t ) L(t) -look Gamma observation model. The bridge time has a direct physical interpretation, and a single L L -conditioned network learns the complete range of noise levels. Unlike methods with a fixed endpoint, γ \gamma -Bridge independently controls L in L_{\mathrm{in}} and L out L_{\mathrm{out}} at inference. For real deployment, an estimated effective look number anchors smart-start at the matching bridge state, enabling zero-shot application across multiple SAR sensors without speckle-free references or sensor-specific fine-tuning. The main contributions are summarized as follows. • A look-parametric diffusion bridge with exact Gamma marginals. We formulate multi-look Gamma restoration as a bridge whose time axis is the physical look number L L rather than an abstract noise schedule. The Gamma–Lévy decomposition yields a closed-form reverse posterior in both stochastic and deterministic forms. • Two orthogonal look-number controls at inference. Target- L L output control terminates the reverse chain at any L out L_{\mathrm{out}} , and smart-start input control anchors an observation with look number L in L_{\mathrm{in}} to the matching bridge state. A single model trained at L obs = 1 L_{\mathrm{obs}}=1 thus performs zero-shot restoration over the full admissible ( L in , L out ) (L_{\mathrm{in}},L_{\mathrm{out}}) grid. Observation conditioning and a two-step consistency loss further stabilize multi-step inference in the low-SNR single-look regime. • Zero-shot transfer to real SAR with distributional validation. Trained only on natural images with synthetic Gamma corruption, γ \gamma -Bridge combines a homogeneous-patch L ^ \hat{L} estimator with smart-start to process data from six spaceborne and airborne SAR sensors without sensor-specific fine-tuning, achieving leading results on standard synthetic benchmarks. Beta-coupled ratio statistics further validate the fidelity of the intermediate Gamma marginals at every reverse step.

sections.heading: II-A Diffusion Models and Non-Gaussian Gamma Processes
sections.text: SAR-DDPM [ 4 ] uses conditional Gaussian diffusion; SDDPM [ 5 ] derives Gaussian forward and reverse processes under multiplicative corruption; S 4 DM [ 6 ] performs self-supervised score estimation after a log-domain transformation; and DA-PhysDiff [ 19 ] introduces a physics-informed LogGamma stochastic differential equation. None of these formulations exposes ( L in , L out ) (L_{\mathrm{in}},L_{\mathrm{out}}) as independently settable physical endpoint parameters. Non-Gaussian diffusion can better reflect image-formation statistics. DDGM [ 7 ] adds centered Gamma residual noise to a generative diffusion rather than modeling multiplicative speckle directly, while star-shaped DDPMs [ 20 ] accommodate exponential-family variables, including Beta and Wishart distributions. Xie et al. [ 8 ] treat Gaussian, Gamma, and Poisson degradations; their Gamma chain uses shape parameters α 0 = ∞ > α 1 > ⋯ > α N \alpha_{0}{=}\infty>\alpha_{1}>\cdots>\alpha_{N} and the Beta-thinning transition x t + 1 = ( α t / α t + 1 ) ​ ζ t + 1 ​ x t x_{t+1}=(\alpha_{t}/\alpha_{t+1})\zeta_{t+1}x_{t} , with ζ t + 1 ∼ Beta ⁡ ( α t + 1 , α t − α t + 1 ) \zeta_{t+1}\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha_{t+1},\alpha_{t}-\alpha_{t+1}) . This construction parallels the independent-Gamma ratio identity underlying our Gamma–Lévy decomposition. The key distinction from Xie et al. is twofold. First, we replace the abstract shape parameter α t \alpha_{t} with the physical look number L ⁡ ( t ) L(t) , so bridge time acquires a direct radar-imaging interpretation and becomes an admissible inference-time control axis. Second, we cast the process as a bridge terminating at the observation x obs x_{\text{obs}} rather than a generative chain terminating at a fixed prior, which admits smart-start input control at any L in ∈ [ L obs , L max ] L_{\mathrm{in}}\in[L_{\mathrm{obs}},L_{\mathrm{max}}] . Observation conditioning and two-step consistency regularize reversal at L obs = 1 L_{\mathrm{obs}}=1 , and Beta-coupled ratio statistics assess the fidelity of intermediate Gamma marginals.

sections.heading: II-B Diffusion Bridges and Trajectory Consistency
sections.text: I 2 SB [ 18 ] uses degraded images as informative endpoints; Denoising Diffusion Bridge Models [ 21 ] learn endpoint-conditioned score transport; and UNSB [ 22 ] handles unpaired translation. DBIM [ 23 ] accelerates bridge sampling, whereas RDBM [ 24 ] spatially adapts restoration through residual-modulated perturbations. All of these formulations rely on Gaussian or Brownian perturbations, so their forward marginals are not physically meaningful outside the target endpoint; γ \gamma -Bridge instead preserves exact Gamma marginals at every step, and every intermediate state is a physically valid L ⁡ ( t ) L(t) -look image. Consistency Models target one- or few-step generation, Consistency Trajectory Models [ 25 ] map arbitrary times along a probability-flow ODE, and GCTMs [ 26 ] extend such maps to arbitrary distribution pairs and image restoration. Our two-step consistency plays a different role: it is a trajectory-level regularizer that provides a training signal ℒ rec \mathcal{L}_{\text{rec}} cannot—at the pointwise ℓ 1 \ell_{1} optimum, ∇ θ ℒ rec = 0 \nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\text{rec}}=0 while ℒ cons \mathcal{L}_{\text{cons}} retains a non-trivial gradient along the reverse chain.

sections.heading: II-C Model-Based and Learning-Based SAR Despeckling
sections.text: Classical SAR despeckling includes local statistical filters [ 27 , 28 ] , nonlocal methods based on probabilistic patch similarity [ 29 , 30 , 31 ] , and variational approaches using constrained optimization or variance stabilization [ 32 , 33 ] . Learning-based methods include supervised networks trained with synthetic speckle [ 11 , 12 ] and semi- or self-supervised methods that avoid clean SAR references [ 14 , 34 , 15 ] . More recent approaches learn real-speckle distributions from unpaired data [ 13 ] or combine noise estimation with Transformer-based refinement [ 35 ] . In all these methods the training objective fixes a single target noise level, and the physical look number L L never appears as an inference-time variable; consequently the input and output speckle levels cannot be adjusted independently at test time.

A predictor that is marginally unbiased at every t t can still produce trajectories with the wrong joint law: two predictions x ^ 0 ​ ( x t , x obs ) \hat{x}_{0}(x_{t},x_{\mathrm{obs}}) and x ^ 0 ​ ( x t ′ , x obs ) \hat{x}_{0}(x_{t^{\prime}},x_{\mathrm{obs}}) obtained at different steps of the same trajectory need not be consistent with each other, and their disagreement propagates into the joint distribution of ( x T − 1 , … , x 0 ) (x_{T-1},\ldots,x_{0}) . The consistency loss ℒ cons \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cons}} (Eq. ( 14 )) supplies a trajectory-level training signal aligned with Prop. 3 , reconstructing x 0 x_{0} from the state reached by advancing the deterministic posterior from t t to t ′ t^{\prime} . Remark 4 (Scope of ℒ cons \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cons}} ) . ℒ cons \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cons}} is defined along the deterministic trajectory (Eq. ( 13 )), so it enforces trajectory consistency for the deterministic reverse of Eq. ( 8 ), whereas Prop. 3 concerns the stochastic chain Eq. ( 6 ). The two are aligned in structure—both are joint-level statements about how predictions at different bridge times must agree—but deterministic-reverse consistency does not formally entail stochastic-chain joint-law fidelity. Empirically, combining ℒ cons \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cons}} with ℒ rec \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}} keeps the reverse trajectory on-manifold and improves multi-step inference in the single-look regime (Section IV-C ); a stochastic-chain consistency loss remains an open direction. Remark 5 (Contrast with Gaussian bridges) . Unlike I 2 SB [ 18 ] , which uses a Brownian-bridge SDE with Gaussian transition kernels, our posterior derives from the additivity of independent Gamma random variables (Lemma 2 ). Two structural consequences follow: (i) samples remain strictly positive by construction, so no clipping is needed to enforce the non-negativity of intensity images; (ii) the schedule enters only through the physical look number L ⁡ ( t ) L(t) , giving bridge time an interpretation as an admissible inference-time control axis rather than an abstract signal-to-noise coordinate.

sections.heading: VI Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced γ \gamma -Bridge, a look-parametric diffusion bridge for multiplicative Gamma image restoration, with SAR despeckling as its primary validation setting. Anchored on an exact Gamma–Lévy kernel and indexed by a look-number schedule, the model exposes the noise strength L L as a runtime-controllable dimension in both the input and output directions. A single training at L obs = 1 L_{\mathrm{obs}}{=}1 supports zero-shot restoration over the full admissible ( L in , L out ) (L_{\mathrm{in}},L_{\mathrm{out}}) grid—a capability absent from both prior Gamma denoisers and prior SAR-specific despecklers. The core theoretical contribution—a closed-form Gamma–Lévy reverse posterior with two-step consistency training—enables stable multi-step inference in the low-SNR regime and improves reconstruction quality over one-step baselines. On real SAR, combining the trained model with a homogeneous-patch L ^ \hat{L} estimator yields zero-shot transfer across six spaceborne and airborne sensors without fine-tuning.

Existing diffusion denoisers parameterize their forward process by abstract signal-to-noise schedules rather than by the physical look number L L , so different deployment scenarios typically require separately trained models, and transfer from synthetic Gamma training to real SAR remains challenging without clean ground truth. We introduce γ \gamma -Bridge, a look-parametric bridge whose schedule L ⁡ ( t ) L(t) connects the noisy observation at L obs L_{\mathrm{obs}} to the clean limit through exact multiplicative Gamma marginals. Its closed-form Gamma–Lévy reverse posterior admits both stochastic and deterministic processes, while observation conditioning and a two-step consistency loss stabilize multi-step inference in the low-SNR single-look regime. Because bridge time directly represents L L , one conditioned network can smart-start from any admissible input look and stop at a target look number. These two orthogonal controls enable zero-shot restoration over the full admissible grid after training only at L obs = 1 L_{\mathrm{obs}}=1 on natural images with synthetic Gamma corruption. Combined with a homogeneous-patch look estimator, γ \gamma -Bridge processes data from six spaceborne and airborne SAR sensors without sensor-specific fine-tuning, achieving leading results on standard synthetic benchmarks while providing physically interpretable input and output controls absent from prior denoisers. I Introduction Multiplicative Gamma noise is a signal-dependent degradation encountered in coherent imaging systems, where it can obscure fine structures and radiometric information. Unlike additive Gaussian noise, its multiplicative and signal-dependent nature makes restoration a distinct image-processing problem. Synthetic aperture radar (SAR) despeckling is a major real-world instance and our primary validation setting. A SAR intensity image is commonly modeled as Y = X ⋅ N Y=X\cdot N , where X X denotes the underlying radar reflectivity and N N is unit-mean Gamma noise with variance 1 / L 1/L . The equivalent number of looks L L determines the noise strength; L = 1 L=1 corresponds to intensity formed from single-look complex (SLC) data at approximately 0 0 dB per-pixel SNR, while multi-look averaging or repeat-pass compositing increases L L , producing cleaner observations at the cost of spatial or temporal resolution. Gamma image restoration has been studied using both model-based and learning-based approaches. Classical log-domain optimization and fractional-diffusion methods suppress Gamma noise while preserving image structures [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . Diffusion-based methods include SAR-DDPM [ 4 ] , SDDPM [ 5 ] , and S 4 DM [ 6 ] , which employ Gaussian or transformed-domain diffusion processes. DDGM [ 7 ] introduces additive Gamma noise, while [ 8 ] formulate Gamma denoising through Beta-thinning. Recent studies unwind speckle with pretrained Gaussian denoisers [ 9 ] , or offer adjustable diffusion-equation smoothing [ 10 ] . However, their diffusion coordinates or control variables are not explicitly exposed as an inference-time axis parameterized by the physical look number. Existing methods generally assume a fixed restoration endpoint or adjust generic smoothing strength, and therefore cannot independently specify the input and output Gamma noise levels through ( L in , L out ) (L_{\mathrm{in}},L_{\mathrm{out}}) at inference time. A further difficulty is that real SAR scenes lack paired speckled and speckle-free ground truth. Supervised learning with synthetic Gamma corruption provides exact targets [ 11 , 12 ] , but may suffer from a gap between idealized noise and sensor- or processing-dependent real SAR statistics [ 13 ] . Semi- and self-supervised methods reduce the need for clean references, yet representative approaches rely on multi-temporal observations, complex-valued measurements, or blind-spot independence assumptions [ 14 , 15 ] . Per-image zero-shot methods avoid external training data but require image-specific optimization and still return a fixed restoration endpoint [ 16 , 17 ] . Thus, label-free inference alone does not establish zero-shot transfer from controlled Gamma training to heterogeneous real SAR sensors without fine-tuning. Since clean real-SAR references remain unavailable, such transfer must also be assessed through distributional and no-reference evidence. This work introduces γ \gamma -Bridge, a look-parametric bridge for general Gamma image restoration, with SAR as its primary real-world application and validation setting. Building on the Gamma-marginal construction of [ 8 ] and image-to-image diffusion bridges [ 18 ] , this work defines a look-number schedule satisfying L ⁡ ( 0 ) = L max L(0)=L_{\mathrm{max}} and L ⁡ ( T − 1 ) = L obs L(T{-}1)=L_{\mathrm{obs}} . Each intermediate state follows x t | x 0 ∼ x 0 ⋅ Gamma ⁡ ( L ⁡ ( t ) , L ⁡ ( t ) ) x_{t}\mid x_{0}\sim x_{0}\cdot\mathrm{Gamma}(L(t),L(t)) and therefore remains consistent with the standard L ⁡ ( t ) L(t) -look Gamma observation model. The bridge time has a direct physical interpretation, and a single L L -conditioned network learns the complete range of noise levels. Unlike methods with a fixed endpoint, γ \gamma -Bridge independently controls L in L_{\mathrm{in}} and L out L_{\mathrm{out}} at inference. For real deployment, an estimated effective look number anchors smart-start at the matching bridge state, enabling zero-shot application across multiple SAR sensors without speckle-free references or sensor-specific fine-tuning. The main contributions are summarized as follows. • A look-parametric diffusion bridge with exact Gamma marginals. We formulate multi-look Gamma restoration as a bridge whose time axis is the physical look number L L rather than an abstract noise schedule. The Gamma–Lévy decomposition yields a closed-form reverse posterior in both stochastic and deterministic forms. • Two orthogonal look-number controls at inference. Target- L L output control terminates the reverse chain at any L out L_{\mathrm{out}} , and smart-start input control anchors an observation with look number L in L_{\mathrm{in}} to the matching bridge state. A single model trained at L obs = 1 L_{\mathrm{obs}}=1 thus performs zero-shot restoration over the full admissible ( L in , L out ) (L_{\mathrm{in}},L_{\mathrm{out}}) grid. Observation conditioning and a two-step consistency loss further stabilize multi-step inference in the low-SNR single-look regime. • Zero-shot transfer to real SAR with distributional validation. Trained only on natural images with synthetic Gamma corruption, γ \gamma -Bridge combines a homogeneous-patch L ^ \hat{L} estimator with smart-start to process data from six spaceborne and airborne SAR sensors without sensor-specific fine-tuning, achieving leading results on standard synthetic benchmarks. Beta-coupled ratio statistics further validate the fidelity of the intermediate Gamma marginals at every reverse step. II Related Work II-A Diffusion Models and Non-Gaussian Gamma Processes SAR-DDPM [ 4 ] uses conditional Gaussian diffusion; SDDPM [ 5 ] derives Gaussian forward and reverse processes under multiplicative corruption; S 4 DM [ 6 ] performs self-supervised score estimation after a log-domain transformation; and DA-PhysDiff [ 19 ] introduces a physics-informed LogGamma stochastic differential equation. None of these formulations exposes ( L in , L out ) (L_{\mathrm{in}},L_{\mathrm{out}}) as independently settable physical endpoint parameters. Non-Gaussian diffusion can better reflect image-formation statistics. DDGM [ 7 ] adds centered Gamma residual noise to a generative diffusion rather than modeling multiplicative speckle directly, while star-shaped DDPMs [ 20 ] accommodate exponential-family variables, including Beta and Wishart distributions. Xie et al. [ 8 ] treat Gaussian, Gamma, and Poisson degradations; their Gamma chain uses shape parameters α 0 = ∞ > α 1 > ⋯ > α N \alpha_{0}{=}\infty>\alpha_{1}>\cdots>\alpha_{N} and the Beta-thinning transition x t + 1 = ( α t / α t + 1 ) ​ ζ t + 1 ​ x t x_{t+1}=(\alpha_{t}/\alpha_{t+1})\zeta_{t+1}x_{t} , with ζ t + 1 ∼ Beta ⁡ ( α t + 1 , α t − α t + 1 ) \zeta_{t+1}\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha_{t+1},\alpha_{t}-\alpha_{t+1}) . This construction parallels the independent-Gamma ratio identity underlying our Gamma–Lévy decomposition. The key distinction from Xie et al. is twofold. First, we replace the abstract shape parameter α t \alpha_{t} with the physical look number L ⁡ ( t ) L(t) , so bridge time acquires a direct radar-imaging interpretation and becomes an admissible inference-time control axis. Second, we cast the process as a bridge terminating at the observation x obs x_{\text{obs}} rather than a generative chain terminating at a fixed prior, which admits smart-start input control at any L in ∈ [ L obs , L max ] L_{\mathrm{in}}\in[L_{\mathrm{obs}},L_{\mathrm{max}}] . Observation conditioning and two-step consistency regularize reversal at L obs = 1 L_{\mathrm{obs}}=1 , and Beta-coupled ratio statistics assess the fidelity of intermediate Gamma marginals. II-B Diffusion Bridges and Trajectory Consistency I 2 SB [ 18 ] uses degraded images as informative endpoints; Denoising Diffusion Bridge Models [ 21 ] learn endpoint-conditioned score transport; and UNSB [ 22 ] handles unpaired translation. DBIM [ 23 ] accelerates bridge sampling, whereas RDBM [ 24 ] spatially adapts restoration through residual-modulated perturbations. All of these formulations rely on Gaussian or Brownian perturbations, so their forward marginals are not physically meaningful outside the target endpoint; γ \gamma -Bridge instead preserves exact Gamma marginals at every step, and every intermediate state is a physically valid L ⁡ ( t ) L(t) -look image. Consistency Models target one- or few-step generation, Consistency Trajectory Models [ 25 ] map arbitrary times along a probability-flow ODE, and GCTMs [ 26 ] extend such maps to arbitrary distribution pairs and image restoration. Our two-step consistency plays a different role: it is a trajectory-level regularizer that provides a training signal ℒ rec \mathcal{L}_{\text{rec}} cannot—at the pointwise ℓ 1 \ell_{1} optimum, ∇ θ ℒ rec = 0 \nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\text{rec}}=0 while ℒ cons \mathcal{L}_{\text{cons}} retains a non-trivial gradient along the reverse chain. II-C Model-Based and Learning-Based SAR Despeckling Classical SAR despeckling includes local statistical filters [ 27 , 28 ] , nonlocal methods based on probabilistic patch similarity [ 29 , 30 , 31 ] , and variational approaches using constrained optimization or variance stabilization [ 32 , 33 ] . Learning-based methods include supervised networks trained with synthetic speckle [ 11 , 12 ] and semi- or self-supervised methods that avoid clean SAR references [ 14 , 34 , 15 ] . More recent approaches learn real-speckle distributions from unpaired data [ 13 ] or combine noise estimation with Transformer-based refinement [ 35 ] . In all these methods the training objective fixes a single target noise level, and the physical look number L L never appears as an inference-time variable; consequently the input and output speckle levels cannot be adjusted independently at test time.
